item.title: India separates Hasina’s return from extradition
item.description:
NEW DELHI: India’s foreign ministry said on Wednesday that former Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina’s plan to return voluntarily to her home country is separate from Dhaka’s extradition request.

Hasina has said that she plans to return home from more than two years of exile in India on Dec 16.

The Bangladesh government, however, reiterated that she can only be extradited.

Hasina fled Dhaka after a deadly student uprising against her rule in Aug 2024 and has lived in exile in India since.

This month, she requested a new passport and identity card so she could return from self-imposed exile.

In Bangladesh, she faces a death sentence handed down in her absence last year by a court that convicted her of ordering a crackdown on the student-led uprising.

Indian foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal reiterated that New Delhi is examining the extradition request by Dhaka in line with its established processes.

“The case of a citizen willing to return voluntarily to her country on a travel document is a matter separate from the extradition request,” Jaiswal said, responding to a question at a regular media briefing. He did not elaborate.

New tensions have risen in Bangladesh after Dhaka rejected Hasina’s request for a passport that would allow her to return.

item.title: Bangladesh ties of 'great importance' to Pakistan, President and PM tell visiting parliament speaker
item.description:
Bangladesh Parliament Speaker Hafizuddin Ahmad on Wednesday met with President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif in Islamabad, where the Pakistani leaders reaffirmed that Islamabad attached “great importance” to its ties with Dhaka.

The parliament speaker, accompanied by a parliamentary delegation, arrived in the country on Monday on a six-day official visit at the special invitation of National Assembly Speaker Sardar Ayaz Sadiq. This is the first official visit to Pakistan by a speaker of the Bangladesh parliament, according to the PM Office (PMO).

On Wednesday, Ahmad and his delegation called on President Zardari at Aiwan-i-Sadr, where the president noted that “Pakistan attaches great importance to its relations with Bangladesh, which are rooted in shared history, common faith and deep cultural and familial affinities”, his office said.

The Bangladeshi delegation included MP Jahrat Adib Chowdhury, chairman of the standing committee on foreign affairs; MPs Humam Quader Chowdhury, Muhammad Nazibur Rahman, Nilufar Chowdhury Moni, and Nasser Rahman; as well as Bangladesh High Commissioner to Pakistan Iqbal Hussain Khan.

On Pakistan’s side, the meeting was attended by Sadiq, Senators Sherry Rehman and Saleem Mandviwalla, MNAs Naveed Qamar and Dr Shazia Sobia Aslam Soomro, along with the convener of the Pakistan-Bangladesh Parliamentary Friendship Group in NA.

Later, PM Shehbaz hosted a dinner at the PM House in honour of the visiting speaker and members of the parliamentary delegation.

“Welcoming the speaker and his delegation, the prime minister said that Pakistan attaches great importance to its fraternal ties with Bangladesh,” PMO said.

Recalling the shared history and cultural affinities between the two countries, the premier underscored the importance of closer institutional cooperation and stronger people-to-people contacts.

The prime minister noted that the “extensive engagements of the visiting parliamentary delegation in Pakistan indicate a huge scope of collaboration in parliamentary domain”, PMO said.

He emphasised that regular parliamentary exchanges would provide a robust foundation for closer bilateral cooperation across various avenues of mutual interest.

PMO also shared pictures of PM Shehbaz individually meeting the members of the visiting delegation.

‘Pakistan ready to extend defence cooperation with Bangladesh’

During his meeting with the visiting delegation, President Zardari emphasised the need to strengthen Pakistan-Bangladesh relations through expanded parliamentary exchanges, trade and economic cooperation, educational links and people-to-people contacts, calling for a “forward-looking approach based on sovereign equality, mutual respect and mutual benefit”.

He noted the “renewed momentum in bilateral relations, particularly in high-level exchanges, education, trade, culture and people-to-people contacts”, the Presidency said.

The president expressed hope for the early finalisation of around 26 memorandums of understanding (MoUs) “under consideration, which would provide an institutional framework for expanding bilateral cooperation”.

He “reaffirmed Pakistan’s readiness to extend defence cooperation with Bangladesh”, also highlighting the “considerable potential” for cooperation in agriculture, industry, food security, disaster management, digital governance and space research.

On connectivity, President Zardari welcomed the commencement in January of direct flights by Biman Bangladesh Airlines and emphasised the need to increase flight frequency and destinations in view of growing demand. He also called for exploring direct maritime links to facilitate trade and economic cooperation.

Discussing trade and economic relations, the president noted that bilateral trade remained below its potential.

Therefore, he called for effectively utilising existing mechanisms, including the Joint Economic Commission (JEC) and the Joint Working Group on Trade, to explore preferential trade arrangements and advance the priority areas identified during the JEC session held in October last year.

President Zardari noted that ongoing exports of Pakistani rice under the government-to-government agreement could serve as a basis for broader cooperation on food security and the supply of essential commodities.

“Pakistan, in line with Bangladesh’s request, is also ready to provide technical expertise for the refurbishment of sugar plants in Bangladesh,” the Presidency statement read.

President Zardari encouraged greater private-sector engagement across a range of sectors, including textiles, pharmaceuticals, leather, automobiles, construction materials, minerals, chemicals, ceramics and jute.

He offered Pakistan’s assistance in facilitating training for Bangladeshi parliamentary officials at the Pakistan Institute for Parliamentary Services (PIPS) and sharing its institutional expertise in operating a bicameral legislature.

The president expressed Islamabad’s desire to further strengthen parliamentary cooperation with Dhaka, as well as highlighted bilateral cooperation in the education and media sectors.

President Zardari welcomed progress under the China-Bangladesh-Pakistan Trilateral Mechanism, particularly the identification of 12 priority areas of cooperation during the Kunming meeting on June 19, 2025, the statement said.

He appreciated Bangladesh’s humanitarian gesture of hosting over one million Rohingya refugees, reaffirmed Pakistan’s support for their safe, voluntary and dignified return to Myanmar in accordance with international law, and called upon the international community to ensure sustained humanitarian assistance.

The president expressed confidence that Ahmad’s visit would help advance bilateral relations and pave the way for more high-level exchanges between the two countries.

Meanwhile, Ahmad thanked the president for the warm welcome and hospitality extended to him and his delegation, according to the President House.

The speaker conveyed the greetings of Bangladesh President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir and Prime Minister Tarique Rahman.

The statement said: “Recalling his personal memories of Pakistan, he underscored the importance of parliamentary diplomacy and expressed his desire to promote closer engagement between the two Parliaments through exchanges and regular institutional interaction.

“He also noted the popularity of Pakistani television dramas in Bangladesh, reflecting the cultural affinity between the peoples of the two countries.”

Relations between Islamabad and Dhaka have improved since the ouster of former Bangladeshi premier Sheikh Hasina, during whose tenure ties between the two countries remained shaky.

In February, Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal attended the oath-taking ceremony of PM Rahman of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP).

Sadiq travelled to Dhaka in December 2025 for the funeral of the country’s first female prime minister Khaleda Zia. In August that year, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar had also visited Dhaka and met Yunus.

item.title: US unveils proposed tariffs on major partners, including EU, China and India
item.description:
The United States on Wednesday unveiled proposed tariffs on 14 economies, including the European Union, China and India, after a months-long probe into alleged excess production — the latest move by US President Donald Trump to remake Washington’s trade relationships.

The duties, proposed at up to 20 per cent, come over allegations that the economies “are promoting production and capacity divorced from the realities of demand and market principles,” a senior US official said on condition of anonymity.

The new tariffs will need to undergo a period of public comment before taking effect, with the official adding that the proposals take existing trade deals into account.

The new levies target some of the United States’ largest trading partners, including China, the European Union, India, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam.

The US official made specific mention of China, for whom a 20pc tariff is being proposed, the joint-highest for any economy.

In a separate announcement, the US Trade Representative’s office also proposed additional tariffs on goods from Brazil, including aircraft, over alleged inaction on addressing US trade concerns.

Trump’s tariffs have targeted Washington’s friends and foes alike, and are part of a push in his second term to remake global trade by forcing countries to buy US products or produce their goods in his country.

The latest move offers some relief for partners that earlier signed tariff deals with the Trump administration, but it could still raise temperatures as the US president prepares to host G20 leaders in Miami in December.

“We don’t expect this to create tension or rancor” at the G20 summit, the senior US official said. “We actually expect that we may be signing more agreements at the G20 in the wake of these announcements.”

Inflation pressures

Over-capacity concerns affect a range of sectors, from batteries to cement, chemicals to processed food, the senior US official said.

The duties could add further pressure on US businesses already squeezed by earlier tariffs, with firms now likelier to pass on costs to consumers already frustrated with the high cost of living.

Affordability was a key issue in recent midterm elections, which saw Trump’s Republican Party swept out of power in both houses of Congress by Democrats.

US consumer inflation came in at 3.7pc year-on-year in September, close to a three-year high as prices are pushed up by the effects of Trump’s war on Iran, tariffs, and the massive AI investment boom.

US Federal Reserve policymakers, responsible for keeping inflation to a long-term two-per cent target, say that most price effects of Trump’s previous tariff rollout have passed through the economy — but any new levies could push prices up further.

The new tariffs are likely to come into effect in January at the earliest, the senior US official said.

Trump’s latest duties come after an investigation the US Trade Representative started in March on excess manufacturing capacity and production.

The concern was whether other countries were taking actions deemed “unreasonable or discriminatory,” and if they weighed on US commerce.

The probes came days after the US Supreme Court struck down Trump’s previous slew of tariffs, holding that the president did not hold the authority to impose the duties using the law the White House had cited.

Pushback expected

Trade lawyer Ryan Majerus told AFP that he expected this probe to be among “the most important” actions for the Trump administration, given its underlying concern that factories with excess capacity start operations abroad and “never get turned off, even if there’s no demand.”

This potentially leads to an oversupply of goods, depressed prices and a “hollowing out” of US manufacturing, he added.

The US determination is likely to face strong pushback from China and others, with Beijing long rejecting criticism that it relies too much on exports to boost its economy.

While the US Supreme Court struck down Trump’s global tariffs in February, his sector-specific duties remain intact.

The new tariffs will not stack on top of those sector-specific tariffs on items like automobiles and steel, the senior US official said.

In July, Trump imposed a separate wave of tariffs on 60 economies, accusing them of insufficient action against forced labour.

For economies facing both the forced labour and excess production tariffs, the levies would not stack, the US official said. Instead, the higher rate of the two would prevail.

item.title: Why Israel should be afraid of the ICJ genocide ruling against Myanmar
item.description:
Why Israel should be afraid of the ICJ genocide ruling against Myanmar

Submitted by Jonathan Cook on Tue, 11/24/2026 - 10:57
The court's finding against Myanmar undercuts each of Israel's defences over Gaza, and exposes the western states that cheered one verdict while arming the other genocide
Pro-Palestinian protesters demonstrate outside the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague, on 24 May, 2024 (Reuters)
Off

There are many reasons why Israel will be deeply worried by the International Court of Justice's finding on 19 November that the military junta in Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority nearly a decade ago.

The president of the world's highest court, Yuji Iwasawa, concluded that Myanmar had the "intention to destroy" a substantial part of the Rohingya population and tried to hide its crimes through "extensive destruction of evidence".

During so-called "clearance operations" in 2017, Myanmar's security forces from the Buddhist-majority state of Myanmar killed at least 10,000 Rohingya, a Muslim minority, and drove more than 700,000 from their homes in northern Rakhine state. Most found refuge in Bangladesh.

Entire villages were erased, evidence destroyed by burning bodies and bulldozing sites, and the Rohingya subjected to campaigns of rape and sexual violence. Myanmar failed to prosecute the perpetrators.

So what are the implications for another prominent genocide case being considered by the ICJ, this one brought against Israel by South Africa, and backed by more than a dozen other countries, including Ireland, Belgium, Spain and the Netherlands?

Back in January 2024, just weeks into Israel's onslaught in Gaza, the World Court found a "plausible risk" that Palestinians there were being subjected to genocide.

It also imposed a series of provisional measures on Israel to ensure its military did not commit genocidal acts, that aid was allowed in, that all incitement stopped, and that the destruction of evidence was prevented. Israel ignored all of these obligations.

Intent on show

First, the ICJ ruling against Myanmar has set a legal precedent. It is the first time the court has found a state guilty of genocide. It clears a path for the United Nations court to make the same finding, based on even more damning evidence, against Israel.

The bar for establishing genocide has always been higher than for proving war crimes or crimes against humanity because, critically, it requires demonstrating intent by the state under investigation.

In ruling against Myanmar, the court noted that the regime had encouraged anti-Rohingya hate speech, portraying the minority as "sub-human" and posing a "violent threat". This rhetoric, in the view of the judges, exposed the deeper reasoning behind Myanmar's "clearance operations".

In Israel's case, it should be easier to establish intent than it was with Myanmar. Nine pages of South Africa's 84-page submission (59-67) to the ICJ were quotes from Israeli leaders, from the prime minister down, expressing genocidal intent towards Gaza's civilian population.

As is often pointed out, this was the most publicly confessed crime in history.

Israel could carry out operations to eradicate Hamas, or disarm it, and still be committing genocide

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu compared Gaza's Palestinians to Amalek. In the Bible, the Israelites are ordered by God to kill every last Amalek man, woman and child, leaving no one alive. In other words, to commit a genocide.

Former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant called the people of Gaza "human animals" and insisted they be denied all food, water and fuel.

President Isaac Herzog declared no one in Gaza, not even its children, to be innocent: "It is an entire nation out there that is responsible. It is not true this rhetoric about civilians not aware, not involved. It's absolutely not true."

The record of genocidal incitement by Israel's leadership is indisputable.

Second, the ICJ rejected Myanmar's defence that its violence was a justifiable response - that it was counterterrorism - following violent attacks by fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army.

The judges ruled that the junta could be pursuing more than one strategy at the same time, and that its military actions to kill rebel fighters could run in parallel to a wider policy of targeting the civilian population.

This is precisely where Israel's narrative is likely to come unstuck.

Israel and its apologists prefer to start the clock with Hamas's one-day breakout on 7 October 2023 from long-besieged Gaza - effectively a concentration camp for Palestinians engineered by Israel over the preceding decades.

Hamas's short, bloody attack inside Israel did not initiate the violence. As the ICJ found in a separate advisory opinion in 2024, Israel has committed crimes systematically against the Palestinian people for decades - and long before October 2023.

That includes an illegal and brutal military occupation, the forced transfer of Palestinians from their homes so Jewish settlers can colonise their land, the prolonged siege of Gaza, and a violent regime of apartheid rule against Palestinians.

More specifically, Israel has claimed its carpet-bombing of Gaza, and its destruction of essential civilian infrastructure - homes, hospitals, schools, government offices, bakeries, agricultural land - is warranted by its efforts to "eradicate Hamas".

In the Myanmar ruling, the ICJ showed it is likely to give short shrift to such rationalisations.

Israel could carry out operations to eradicate Hamas, or disarm it, and still be committing genocide. In fact, it could do so precisely to remove the possibility of resistance to its war crimes and make the task of committing genocide easier.

Cover story

Third, Myanmar argued that, if its goal was genocide, it could have killed far more Rohingya than it actually did. Estimates are that the junta's actions most likely killed between 1 and 2 percent of the Rohingya people.

The ICJ found, in accordance with the 1948 Genocide Convention, that genocide is not a numbers game. Once intent to destroy a people in whole or part is established, other practices - such as preventing births, forcibly displacing the population, and making their lands uninhabitable - also qualify as genocide.

Israel and its apologists have wilfully sought to mislead about the convention's definition, treating the Holocaust as the only model of what a genocide looks like.

Israel's genocide in Gaza continues. So must the protests
Read More »

Their argument rests heavily on the false idea that genocide is indeed about numbers, and that Israel would have wiped out everyone in Gaza were it actually bent on genocide.

Netanyahu has regularly articulated this sentiment. In August 2025, for example, he told a press conference: "If we had wanted to commit genocide, it would have taken exactly one afternoon."

Again, the ICJ is unlikely to entertain this as a defence.

Netanyahu's logic intentionally obscures the obvious fact that, in an age of international law, states like Myanmar and Israel have a vested interest in concealing their genocidal intent both by carrying out their crimes incrementally and by offering military rationales as a cover story.

Based on the Rohingya ruling, the number of dead in Gaza is sufficient to qualify as genocidal violence. The known death toll, at nearly 75,000, is more than 3 percent of Gaza's population - and double the percentage of known Rohingya fatalities at the hands of Myanmar's junta.

The Gaza estimates, however, are likely to be a severe undercount, given that many Palestinians were buried under rubble or vaporised by US-supplied 2,000lb bombs. It is also a count of those killed by Israeli weaponry, not those who have died as a result of the dire conditions Israel has engineered in the enclave.

The Israeli military's own assessments are also damning. According to their tally, revealed in August 2025, more than four in five of the dead were civilians, not Palestinian fighters.

Genetic harm

Fourth, the ICJ found that Myanmar had committed genocide in three of the convention's five categories: the mass killing; causing serious bodily and mental harm through torture, physical injuries and sexual violence; and preventing births within the group by targeting children and reproductive organs.

Israel has clearly committed crimes on a significant scale in these same three categories, plus it has violated an additional, fourth category of the convention.

As noted earlier, both numerically and proportionally, Israel has killed more Palestinians than Myanmar killed Rohingya. UN bodies have repeatedly found that Israel has caused serious bodily and mental harm to the people of Gaza.

Nearly one in ten Palestinians there are known to have been maimed by Israel's attacks, and nearly everyone has been left with deep mental scars from Israel's relentless bombing campaigns, the equivalent of unleashing at least six Hiroshimas over the tiny enclave.

In addition, thousands of Palestinians - men, women and children - have been seized from Gaza and held in detention camps where torture and sexual violence are reported to be rife. Inmates often emerge severely malnourished.

In June, a UN commission of inquiry concluded that Israel was deliberately targeting children in Gaza. It said these acts "form part of a deliberate strategy to destroy the future of the Palestinians in Gaza by targeting their children".

Independent witnesses, such as international doctors volunteering in Gaza, have testified that soldiers appear to be playing horrifying games in which they compete with each other to show off their prowess as snipers.

Each day, according to the doctors, the soldiers target a different body part: the neck, the abdomen, the testicles.

The ICJ also has plenty of evidence to find against Israel in an additional category in the Genocide Convention, that of creating conditions destructive to life.

In Myanmar's case, the ICJ ruled that evidence the Rohingya had been confined in internment camps where they were denied basic healthcare was not sufficient to meet this fourth category.

In Israel's case, by contrast, Palestinians have not only been denied access to health services. Israel has systematically gone about destroying the entire healthcare system and blocking the entry of medicines and medical equipment.

It has subjected the people of Gaza to sustained starvation, creating widespread malnutrition that scientists warn will cause lasting genetic harm.

It has blocked the entry of equipment to repair water and sewage systems Israel has destroyed, exposing the people to contaminated groundwater and the spread of disease. It has also blocked tents, blankets and mattresses desperately needed as winter sets in.

As Oxfam and the Conflict and Environment Observatory reported on 23 November, by reducing Gaza's buildings to rubble through the use of many tens of thousands of tonnes of explosives, Israel has created a "toxic wasteland", one that will expose the enclave's inhabitants to grave health dangers for "generations to come".

On these and many other grounds, the ICJ can find Israel has violated the Genocide Convention even more comprehensively than Myanmar.

Journalists killed

Fifth, as part of the genocide finding against Myanmar, the World Court factored in a wider context of systematic discrimination by Buddhist majority against the Rohingya that reinforced suspicions of genocidal intent.

These discriminatory policies included eroding the Rohingya's human rights through restrictions on movement and the blocking of humanitarian aid, and limiting married couples to two children.

Other matters served similarly as circumstantial evidence, especially the concealment and destruction of evidence, a failure to prevent civilians from committing atrocities alongside security forces, and a reluctance to prosecute perpetrators.

As noted earlier, the ICJ has already found Israel guilty of operating a decades-old system of apartheid against Palestinians. That included blockading Gaza by land, sea and air for nearly two decades, strictly controlling who could go in or out of the enclave.

Israel has repeatedly been caught in lies designed to cover up its atrocities

Israel was also forced to admit in 2012 that it had imposed a near-starvation diet on the people of Gaza starting four years earlier. In the words of a close adviser to the prime minister of the time, Ehud Olmert, the goal was "to put the Palestinians on a diet, but not to make them die of hunger".

In 2015, the UN warned that Gaza, under Israel's severe restrictions, would soon become "uninhabitable", that Israel had sought to de-develop the enclave, and that the enclave's aquifers were quickly becoming contaminated by seawater, posing a threat to the health of the population.

Israel has sought to conceal its crimes in Gaza by refusing to allow entry to foreign journalists to report on what is happening there. Meanwhile, it has killed local Palestinian journalists in unprecedented numbers in an attempt to stop them from documenting its crimes.

Israel has repeatedly been caught in lies designed to cover up its atrocities and has sought to destroy incriminating evidence, including by secretly burying Palestinian victims of its violence in mass graves.

The UN found in March 2025, for example, that the Israeli military had buried in a mass grave 15 emergency workers who it had picked off "one by one" after ambushing their vehicles.

The crews had been coming to the aid of another team attacked by the Israeli army earlier that day in Rafah. The UN noted that Israeli bulldozers had crushed the ambulances and then covered them with sand.

Similarly, Israel attacked and seized two large hospitals in Gaza, Nasser and al-Shifa, in early 2024. After its forces pulled out, large mass graves were found close by both.

At Nasser Hospital, three mass graves contained 392 bodies, including those of women, children, the elderly and injured people. Evidence was found of "field executions" and mutilations of some of the dead.

As with Myanmar, such atrocities by Israeli soldiers go uninvestigated and unpunished. Even after a video showed five reservists anally raping a Palestinian prisoner with a baton, causing him severe internal injuries, the Israeli military dropped all charges.

Also like Myanmar, Israel has let civilian groups from its Jewish population collude in its genocidal violence without punishment. Far-right groups have regularly been allowed to mass at crossing points to block the delivery of critically needed food. On repeated occasions, they have looted the aid.

In summer 2024, at the height of these blockades, it was found that three of the groups were being rewarded by Israel and the US with special tax-deductible status for donations.

Hypocrites to the end

In these and all other cases of suspected atrocities, Israel has refused access to outside investigators, just as it has journalists. It has continued that policy even after agreeing to a ceasefire in October 2025 - a ceasefire it has entirely ignored.

More than 1,670 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza during the ceasefire period.

Israel's aversion to transparency is likely to incriminate it further in the eyes of the ICJ's judges, just as it did for Myanmar.

The court has shown in its latest ruling that it is ready to fill evidential gaps, even if it means drawing on arm's-length investigations by UN agencies and international and local human rights bodies. There is a wealth of damning evidence already.

Gaza flooding is a catastrophe by design - and the spineless West is complicit
Read More »

The ICJ is also likely to accept the growing body of confessions made by Israeli soldiers of their involvement in atrocities and the systematic use of violence against the people of Gaza through AI, as set out by whistleblowing intelligence officers in a recent documentary, NAZA.

It is not just Israel, however, that has reasons to be fearful of the Myanmar judgment.

Several western states, including Britain, Canada, France and Germany, backed the genocide case against Myanmar at the ICJ initiated by The Gambia. Separately, the US assessed in 2022 that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya.

On 19 November, Ed Miliband, the UK foreign secretary, welcomed the ICJ ruling, ordered the expulsion of Myanmar's defence attache and threatened "further action". Four days later, Britain formally recognised the genocide and sanctioned five Myanmar generals.

The US noted that it had been the "leading donor for the Rohingya refugee humanitarian response", and that it shared "grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights" of the Rohingya.

Western states' hypocrisy is fully on show. They have failed in their duty to prevent an even more obvious genocide in Gaza than the one in Myanmar, despite the World Court warning them of the "plausible risk" in January 2024.

Not only that, but the genocide in Gaza would have been impossible without active help from the US, Britain and Germany in supplying the weapons used to kill Palestinians en masse, providing intelligence to Israel and offering diplomatic cover.

The case against Myanmar took seven years to reach its conclusion after The Gambia brought it to the ICJ. If a similar timeline is followed in Gaza's case, Israel may not be found guilty for another three or four years.

Israel can do a lot more damage to the enclave and its population in the meantime. The Myanmar case should prove to western states that they need to act now. It should galvanise a response.

Instead, hypocrites to the bitter end, western capitals will carry on backing the current genocide in Gaza as they lament the earlier one in Myanmar.

item.title: UN: Five women killed each hour by relatives in 2025
item.description:
More than 47,000 women and girls, or around five per hour, were killed by relatives around the world in 2025, a figure broadly unchanged from previous years, according to a UN report published Tuesday.
The number of women and girls killed by an intimate partner or a family member has fluctuated between 45,000 and 51,000 over the past several years, according to estimates by UN Women and the UN Office on Drugs and Crime.
Of the 78,000 women and girls who were victims of intentional homicide last year, around 60% were killed by an intimate partner or family member, the report said ahead of the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women.
The estimated 47,000 victims represent 129 women and girls killed every day. The figure was calculated using an analysis of statistics from 122 countries and territories.
While women accounted for 19% of homicide victims worldwide in 2025, 60% of them were killed in the private sphere. By contrast, 11% of male homicide victims were killed in such circumstances.
The UN stressed the "urgency of ensuring that the prevention of domestic violence addresses intimate relationships, as well as relationships in wider family structures."
No region was completely safe but Africa once again recorded the highest number of women and girls killed by intimate partners or family members, at 22,100.
Asia followed with 15,100 victims, ahead of the Americas with 7,400, Europe with 2,100 and Oceania with 300.
The report also noted that while homicide rates have fallen globally, rates of femicide have declined more slowly, particularly in the Americas and Europe.
This suggests, according to the UN, "that these crimes are deeply rooted in social norms and gender stereotypes," adding that it points to barriers in accessing the justice system.
Femicide refers to the gender-related killing of women and girls. Beyond murders committed by intimate partners or family members, the term can also encompass certain killings linked to organized crime, forced labor or human trafficking.
However, data on femicides committed outside the private sphere remain very limited, the report said, making it impossible to measure the scale of the phenomenon at regional or global level.

The force remains committed to ensuring the safety of people's lives and property, keeping normal movement and daily activities uninterrupted, and taking necessary precautionary measures to deal with any untoward situation.

Battery-rickshaw drivers earn Tk 29,000 a month, pay Tk 10,323 in rent
item.description:
A battery-powered rickshaw driver in Dhaka earns an average of Tk 29,000 a month. From this income, the driver has to pay the rickshaw owner an average of Tk 10,323 a month in rent. This means that, on average, 38.6 per cent of their monthly earnings go towards paying the owner.

This information emerged from a joint study by BRAC and the BRAC Institute of Governance and Development (BIGD).

Mehnaz Rabbani, BIGD’s director of operations, presented the findings at a policy dialogue titled ‘Battery-powered rickshaws: Livelihoods and an inclusive, sustainable transition’ at the CIRDAP auditorium in the capital today, Tuesday.

The study, titled ‘The political and socio-economic realities of battery-powered rickshaws in Bangladesh’, collected data from 450 rickshaw drivers in Dhaka and Barishal. Of the drivers surveyed, 78.2 per cent rented their rickshaws, while 18 per cent owned their vehicles. Data for the study were collected in June and July.

Battery-run rickshaws barred from highways, expressways and elevated expressways

The study found that 78.3 per cent of the drivers surveyed in Dhaka had come from other districts. Of them, 84.2 per cent had moved to the capital because of limited job opportunities and limited scope of income in their localities.

Some 42.2 per cent of the drivers surveyed had faced a major livelihood crisis in the previous year. Of these, 87.9 per cent said their income had fallen by more than half or their work had come to a complete halt during the crisis.

They had to take out loans to cope with the situation. If their income stopped, nearly 62.9 per cent of the drivers would be unable to support their families for more than a week.

The study also highlighted the significant number of accidents involving rickshaw drivers. In the month before the survey (May), 26.7 per cent of the drivers had been involved in at least one road accident.

Of the drivers surveyed, 96 per cent did not have a licence. The remaining 4 per cent reportedly drove rickshaws with permits issued by city corporations and organisations for people with disabilities.

The study said that a sudden ban on or restrictions on the operation of battery-powered rickshaws could reduce drivers’ incomes and place considerable pressure on their families. Their livelihoods therefore need to be taken into account when formulating a regulatory framework.

The study examined the ‘Three-Wheeled Low-Speed Battery-Operated Rickshaw (E-Rickshaw) Movement Rules, 2026’ prepared by the Local Government Division. It described the guidelines as an important step towards recognising the sector and bringing it under orderly management.

However, effective implementation would be the main challenge. Alongside road safety, environmental risks and the regulatory framework, the lives and livelihoods of people working in the sector would also have to be considered.

E-rickshaws hit Dhaka streets, but fares remain high

Dhaka South City Corporation Administrator Abdus Salam spoke at the event. He said city residents had the right to move around without hindrance, while rickshaw drivers also had the right to live and work.

However, if everyone continued to head towards Dhaka, ensuring civic amenities would become impossible. The issues therefore needed to be considered together, and an integrated plan drawn up with the involvement of all stakeholders and taking into account the overall capacity of Dhaka city.

Dhaka North City Corporation Administrator Shafiqul Islam Khan said, “We are not against auto-rickshaws or rickshaw drivers. Their right to a livelihood must also be protected. However, if they operate within a set of rules, there will be scope for accountability, and we will be able to support them more effectively.”

Professor Shamsul Hoque of Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (BUET) blamed weaknesses in the public transport system for the growing number of battery-powered rickshaws in the country.

He said Bangladesh had failed to make buses an attractive mode of transport. The metro rail, however, had proved attractive. Even people who owned cars left them at home and travelled by metro rail. This was not because of its speed, but its reliability. No other mode of transport had been able to offer that.

During the panel discussion, Prothom Alo Executive Editor Sajjad Sharif spoke about rising inequality in Bangladesh, the lack of good governance and the excessive centralisation of everything in Dhaka.

He said battery-powered rickshaws were, in fact, a reflection of these problems — a very ugly reflection. He did not believe the issue could be resolved with a few quick fixes.

The study made several recommendations for regulating battery-powered rickshaws. It said safety standards for the vehicles and designated operating areas must be established. It must be clearly specified which roads they can use, how fast they can travel, and where they can park and pick up or drop off passengers.

Auto-rickshaw cannot be given blank cheque as it cannot be stopped

The study also recommended ensuring the safety of electricity connections and charging systems at garages. It said arrangements should be introduced to upgrade garages and bring them under a formal accreditation system where necessary.

A safe system must be developed for collecting, transporting and recycling old batteries. It also recommended considering the potential for using environmentally friendly battery technology and solar power for charging.

BRAC Executive Director Asif Saleh said the voices of people working in the informal sector did not reach policymakers. The challenges surrounding the safety, road management and regulation of battery-powered rickshaws needed to be addressed by taking drivers’ realities into account and ensuring a just transition.

Professor Akhtar Mahmud of the Department of Urban and Regional Planning at Jahangirnagar University, Dhaka Metropolitan Police Joint Commissioner (Traffic-South) Mohammad Asfiqur Rahman Akhtar, and BRAC Director Ahmed Nazmul Hossain, among others, took part in the panel discussion.

BRAC Director Nafiul Hasan moderated a panel discussion during the second session of the event.

item.description:
Nine more children died with measles symptoms in the 24 hours until 8am on Tuesday, while 1,351 suspected and confirmed cases were reported across the country, the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) said.
With the latest fatalities, the number of deaths from suspected measles has risen to 1,256 since March 15. No deaths from confirmed measles were reported during the latest 24-hour period, keeping the confirmed death toll at 105.
The combined death toll from confirmed measles and measles-like symptoms has now reached 1,361 since March 15.
The DGHS said 1,283 suspected cases and 68 confirmed cases were reported in the 24 hours until 8am Tuesday.
Since March 15, the country has recorded 259,190 suspected cases and 26,300 confirmed cases, according to the latest DGHS data.
A total of 231,999 patients with suspected measles have been admitted to hospitals nationwide since March 15. Of them, 223,158 have been discharged, the release added.

item.title: Adviser: Govt discussing Hasina’s return with India, not with her
item.description:
Prime Minister’s Information and Broadcasting Adviser Zahed Ur Rahman on Tuesday said the government had no communication with former prime minister Sheikh Hasina over her return and was holding discussions with India on the issue.
The adviser made the remarks while responding to a question at a briefing at the Secretariat about a Reuters report quoting Hasina's spokesperson that she intended to return to Bangladesh by a Biman Bangladesh Airlines flight on December 16.
Describing Hasina as a convicted criminal, he said the judicial process against her had been completed and she had been found guilty and sentenced, rather than merely facing allegations.
There should be no legal obstacle to the extradition of Sheikh Hasina if she wants to return to Bangladesh, Zahed Ur Rahman said.
“Bangladesh wants her back and Hasina herself wants to return, so India could extradite her as the positions of both sides are now aligned,” said
The adviser said India had previously cited legal issues regarding her extradition, but he did not see any such obstacle now if Hasina herself wanted to return.
“If Sheikh Hasina wants to come to Bangladesh, I don't think there is any reason for her to go to court or face any legal complications. Her lawyers might try various things if she does not want to come. But if she wants to return, India can simply extradite her and let her come. I don't see any problem now,” he said.
Asked about allegations among Awami League leaders and activists that the government might prevent Hasina from returning at the last moment, Zahed said Hasina herself could request India to extradite her if she believed the government did not want her back.
Such a move, he said, would also make the government's position clear.
He also said Hasina's stated intention to return on December 16 might be an attempt to demonstrate the significance of her decision to her political followers.
“It's a bluff to the political people,” he said.
Explaining the agreement between Bangladesh and India, Zahed said the two countries had an extradition treaty, not a prisoner exchange agreement.
He said prisoner exchange generally implied that one country would hand over a prisoner in return for another, whereas extradition did not involve any such exchange.
Asked about arguments that Hasina had not been taken to India by the Indian authorities but had instead been left there by the then Bangladesh government, the adviser said Bangladesh was effectively without a government at the time.
He said there was no government in place until the interim government, led by Dr Muhammad Yunus, took the oath.
Therefore, he said, it would not be appropriate to use that argument to shift responsibility onto the current elected government.

item.title: 174 undocumented Bangladeshis return from Libya
item.description:
A total of 174 undocumented Bangladeshis who were stranded in Libya and wished to return home voluntarily have been repatriated.
They arrived in Dhaka at 4:45am on Tuesday aboard Buraq Air flight UZ-222.
According to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the repatriation was carried out with the joint cooperation of the Bangladesh Embassy in Libya, the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment, the Libyan government and the International Organization for Migration (IOM).
Most of the returnees had entered Libya illegally after being lured and assisted by human traffickers, hoping to reach Europe by sea, the ministry said. Many reportedly faced abduction and torture in Libya.
Officials from the foreign ministry, other relevant ministries and IOM welcomed them at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka.
The foreign ministry urged the returnees to share their harrowing experiences to raise public awareness about the risks of irregular migration.
IOM provided each returnee with travel expenses, food supplies and basic medical care, as well as temporary accommodation where necessary.
The ministry also said it was working with the Bangladesh Embassy in Libya, the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment and IOM to safely repatriate other Bangladeshis held at detention centres across Libya.

item.title: Nepal’s new PM eyes closer ties with India amid lingering disputes
item.description:
For years, Nepal’s relationship with India was shaped by familiar faces, as leaders of the Himalayan country’s erstwhile three major parties took turns in the prime minister’s office through revolving coalition governments.
This week’s state visit to India by Balendra Shah, a 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician, marked a clear break from that pattern.
As a young, first-time prime minister with a strong electoral mandate, Shah represents a new political force in Kathmandu.
But long-standing economic strain, along with August’s devastating flash floods and the Nepalese public’s high hopes for more jobs, investment and better governance at home, have made Shah’s first bilateral visit abroad more than a mere diplomatic box-ticking exercise.
To safeguard Nepal’s flood recovery and development, Shah needs to get off on the right foot with India, his country’s southern neighbor and largest trading partner, and its long-standing prime minister, Narendra Modi.
While Nepal and India share an open border as well as deep cultural and historical ties, their relationship has also been marked by territorial disputes and a desire in Nepal to be seen as an equal by its much larger and more powerful neighbor.
Constantino Xavier, a senior fellow at the Center for Social and Economic Progress in New Delhi, however, cautioned against expecting too much from a single visit.
“We need a big, long-term ambition coupled with small, short-term steps,” he told DW, arguing that economic cooperation should remain the central focus of relations because it directly contributes to the socioeconomic development of both countries.
The young prime minister’s test is to turn a strong domestic electoral mandate and political goodwill with New Delhi into tangible economic gain, as well as to address longstanding border disputes and a massive trade imbalance.
Shah’s administration sees diplomacy as key to addressing the country’s development aspirations, which was reflected in bilateral talks with Modi on Monday.
Economic cooperation featured prominently during the talks as both sides sought engagements in trade, investment, connectivity and infrastructure development.
Kathmandu’s priority was securing Indian financial support for reconstruction following the August disaster that claimed the lives of more than 1,450 people, while 5,745 are missing or unaccounted for.
The floods swept away roads, bridges, hydropower projects and settlements, with reconstruction bills estimated at around $4.8 billion.
At a joint press briefing after their talks in New Delhi, Modi announced a package of $1.63 billion to help rebuild flood-hit areas and upgrade other infrastructure projects — around $380 million as a grant, with the rest as a concessional loan.
The South Asian neighbors also agreed to deepen cooperation across a wide range of areas, including trade, investment, connectivity and people-to-people ties, and launched a new long-term vision aimed at strengthening economic integration and development.
The talks also yielded commitments to broaden educational and innovation partnerships, boost energy and infrastructure cooperation, improve market access and trade links, and enhance landlocked Nepal’s connectivity through additional air and port access via India.
Shah’s visit offered an opportunity to break the ice in a high-level exchange visit and improve a relationship periodically strained by political mistrust, territorial disputes and differing strategic interests.
Nepal and India both have competing territorial claims over Kalapani, Lipulekh and Limpiyadhura, a strategic Himalayan territory in northwestern Nepal.
As mayor of Kathmandu, Shah raised the border disputes with India, which helped boost his nationalist image and set his broader political agenda. However, his India visit steered clear of such contentious issues.
Bimala Rai Paudyal, a former Foreign Minister of Nepal, said Shah avoided tricky bilateral issues to focus on his administration’s economic agenda.
“This visit could be a good starting point towards resolving the border issues that have been the key strain in our relations,” she told DW. “But the new government didn’t show interest or the guts to address this.”
Ashok Swain, head of the Department of Peace and Conflict Research at Sweden’s Uppsala University, said the visit’s success should be measured by whether the two countries can establish a predictable and mutually beneficial relationship.
“Nepal’s territorial disputes, concerns over the 1950 Treaty of Peace and Friendship and its economic and transit dependence on India need to be addressed,” Swain told DW.
“Shah’s biggest opportunity is to transform Nepal’s geographical location between India and China from a strategic vulnerability into an economic and diplomatic asset,” he added, arguing that Nepal should not be forced to choose between its two neighbors.
Whether the visit marks a tangible reset on the economic front will ultimately depend not on the number of agreements announced, but on how they are implemented and whether the two governments are willing to address the disputes that have long strained ties.

item.title: 14 countries ‘acknowledge’ ICJ ruling on Rohingya ‘genocide’
item.description:
The UK and 13 other countries on Monday “acknowledged” the top UN court’s ruling that Myanmar perpetrated genocide against its Rohingya minority as London announced new sanctions.
The foreign ministers of Australia, Belgium, Canada, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Estonia, Iceland, Latvia, Luxembourg, New Zealand, Portugal, Spain, The Gambia and the United Kingdom said Myanmar had “violated its obligations under the Genocide Convention.”
“We underscore that the Court’s judgment is binding upon Myanmar and call on Myanmar to comply fully with its obligations under international law, including the Court’s decision,” they said in a joint statement.
The UK separately said it “formally recognizes” genocide against the Rohingya and announced sanctions on five senior military figures.
“The horrific violence and persecution inflicted on the Rohingya cannot go unanswered,” UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said.
The sanctions include asset freezes and travel bans, a Foreign Office statement said, adding that London “also intends to introduce legislation targeting the export and supply of aviation fuel to Myanmar.”
“The UK is providing an additional £5m in new funding to support Rohingya and other communities with essential lifesaving and life-affirming services to approximately 350,000 people who need it most in Rakhine state, where humanitarian need is most acute,” the statement added.
It said a further £3 million would “go towards strengthening accountability and justice for survivors of human rights abuses across Myanmar.”
On November 19 in a historic verdict, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority during a 2017 crackdown in the western Rakhine state.
The ruling was the first time in the ICJ’s 80-year history that it has determined that a state committed genocide.
Myanmar’s government called the ruling unfair and a “great disappointment.”
Shortly after the verdict, Britain announced it would expel Myanmar’s defense attaché.

item.title: Govt to award laptops to 1,500 top SSC achievers
item.description:
The government has taken an initiative to award laptops to 1,500 meritorious students who secured GPA-5 in all subjects in this year's Secondary School Certificate (SSC) and equivalent examinations.
The initiative was taken by the Secondary and Higher Education Division of the Ministry of Education at the directive of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to recognize their academic excellence and encouraging greater engagement with modern technology.
Under the initiative, the top 100 highest-scoring students from each of the country's 11 education boards will be selected on the basis of merit, taking the total number of initial recipients to 1,100.
An additional 400 laptops will be kept in reserve to accommodate the candidates securing equal marks at the 100th position.
The programme will be implemented under the scheme titled "Strengthening Reading Habit among Secondary Students", under the Secondary Education Development Programme (SEDP) aimed at promoting academic excellence and equipping students with modern technological skills.
The government plans to procure the laptops in accordance with the Public Procurement Rules (PPR)-2025 and distribute them among the selected students by February-March 2027.
Education and Primary and Mass Education Minister Dr ANM Ehsanul Hoque Milon told BSS that the government had decided to initially award laptops to the top 1,500 students selected on merit from the 11 education boards.
"We have decided to provide laptops to the top 1,500 students from the 11 education boards in the initial phase. The programme will be expanded further through various initiatives," he said.
He added that 400 additional laptops had been reserved to address cases where multiple students secured identical marks at the 100th position.
The government is also considering introducing similar incentives for meritorious students at the HSC level.
According to Education Ministry officials, the initial plan was to provide laptops to 40,000 students who secured GPA-5 in all subjects. However, the government has opted for a phased implementation, beginning with 1,500 recipients.
The estimated expenditure for the first phase is Tk16-17 crore.
Professor Md Firoz Alam, director of the scheme, told BSS that the initiative was designed not only to recognise academic achievement but also to familiarise students with artificial intelligence (AI) and modern information technology.
He said the education boards would verify their respective databases and submit the final selection lists to ensure a transparent, merit-based process.
Alam also emphasised that the laptops would have modern features and quality configurations. A formal distribution programme involving all 11 education boards is being planned.
The selection will be determined by students' total marks rather than GPA-5 alone, following the framework developed by the Dhaka Education Board.
Under the distribution formula, 50% of the selected students will come from the science group, 30% from the humanities group and 20% from the business studies group, taking into account the number and proportion of examinees in each group.
Officials said the same formula had been followed by the other eight general education boards, while the Technical Education Board and Madrasa Education Board adopted slightly different selection procedures to reflect their respective academic structures.
Professor Syed Akhtaruzzaman, President of the Inter-Education Board Coordination Committee and Chairman of the Dhaka Education Board, told BSS that the top 100 highest-scoring students from each board had been selected in accordance with the ministry's instructions.
The final lists from all 11 boards had already been submitted to the ministry.
Engr Md Abul Kalam Azad said the lists of top GPA-5 achievers in the SSC Vocational and Dakhil Vocational examinations had been prepared and forwarded to the coordination committee.
He explained that students from the two streams had been selected proportionately, considering the significantly lower number of candidates in Dakhil Vocational compared to SSC Vocational.
Madrasah Education Board Controller of Examinations Professor Md Faruk Ahmed said the board had prepared and submitted a list of the highest-scoring students who secured GPA-5 in all subjects in the Dakhil examination.
He said the selection also considered the proportional representation of students from the science, humanities and Mujabbid groups.
Meanwhile, Director General of the Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education Bangladesh, Dhaka Prof. Dr. Khan Moinuddin Al Mahmud Sohel told BSS that the Ministry of Finance had given its consent to the distribution of laptops among the 1,500 students.
He said the initiative reflected the government's commitment to motivating students to excel academically while enabling them to develop technological competencies essential for higher education and future professional pursuits.
This year, the average pass rate in the SSC and equivalent examinations across the 11 education boards stood at 62.25%, while 116,676 students achieved GPA-5.

item.title: Canada vows faster visas, more jobs for skilled Bangladeshis
item.description:
Canada has pledged to expedite and simplify visa processing for Bangladeshi travellers, students and businesspeople, while expressing interest in recruiting skilled workers from Bangladesh and expanding cooperation in cybersecurity.
The assurances came from Weldon Epp, assistant deputy minister for the Indo-Pacific at Global Affairs Canada, during a courtesy call on Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed at the Secretariat on Tuesday.
Foysal Hasan, deputy chief information officer of the Home Ministry, said the meeting discussed issues of mutual interest, including curbing irregular migration, exporting skilled manpower, cybersecurity, joint investment and resolving the Rohingya crisis.
At the outset, the home minister described Bangladesh and Canada as longstanding friends and development partners.
In response, Epp said that despite efforts to balance its immigration policy, Canada remained interested in welcoming talented Bangladeshi students and skilled professionals.
He assured the minister that visa processing for legitimate travellers, students and businesspeople from Bangladesh would be made faster and easier.
Salahuddin Ahmed urged Canada to recruit skilled workers from Bangladesh through legal channels in line with its labour market needs.
He said Bangladesh had a large pool of trained professionals in nursing, medical technology, home care, marine services and hospitality. Canada could help develop the required workforce by sending trainers to Bangladesh or establishing specialised training academies through joint initiatives.
Welcoming the proposal, Epp said Canada's economy had a growing demand for skilled workers, particularly nurses and caregivers.
The two sides also discussed expanding bilateral trade and investment. The home minister expressed Bangladesh's interest in acquiring advanced technology, including river and coastal patrol vessels for the Coast Guard and cybersecurity and communication equipment for the police.
On the Rohingya crisis, Epp said Canada had increased the number of Rohingya refugees it resettled from Bangladesh despite its efforts to limit overall immigration.
He said Canada was also working to encourage greater involvement by regional countries, particularly members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), in resolving the crisis.

item.title: Why Donald Trump Jr.’s investment firm is the focus of a widening probe in the House
item.description:
A top House Democrat is broadening his investigation into Donald Trump Jr.’s venture capital fund 1789 Capital by demanding records from four companies that secured an investment before benefiting from lucrative federal contracts or policies.

Rep. Jamie Raskin, the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee and the panel’s incoming chair, sent letters on Monday evening to the defense contractor Hadrian Automation, vape maker Juul Labs, prediction market platform Polymarket and the online firearms seller GrabAGun.

The Maryland congressman requested that each firm send him two years’ worth of communications with 1789 Capital and other select documents, saying the materials would help him investigate whether U.S. President Donald Trump’s eldest son used insider information to orchestrate or anticipate government actions that boosted the companies and his own finances.

The investigation was opened over the summer

Both Trump Jr. and 1789 Capital, which is based in Palm Beach, Florida, deny any wrongdoing.

The letters ramp up an investigation that Raskin opened in August into Trump Jr.’s firm, which he said “suddenly struck investment gold” after naming the president’s son as a partner in 2024. As one of the lawmakers who will be spearheading Democrats’ oversight of the Trump administration when they take control of Congress in January, Raskin has said that uncovering information about bribery and financial corruption will be among his top priorities.

Trump Jr. has repeatedly rejected accusations that he has exploited government access for profit. At an Axios event last week, he acknowledged that he understood people’s corruption concerns, but said that they weren’t accurate, noting he has been an investor for decades.

“I can see what they are saying. It doesn’t make it so,” he said. “The notion that I should somehow sit in a corner, suck my thumb and wait, you know, eight years — in this case 12 years — till we’re out of the political game, it’s not real.”

Trump Jr. and the firm deny any wrongdoing

1789 Capital also has forcefully denied claims of wrongdoing. In a letter to Raskin in September, the company’s lawyers defended the firm’s investment thesis as predating Trump’s administration and said that while it “welcomes legitimate congressional oversight,” it “has no intention of being held hostage to political gamesmanship.”

On Monday, the company’s attorney, Bill Burck, said the September letter explained flaws in Raskin’s understanding, but Raskin “never bothered to reply.”

“Facts are facts and Congressman Raskin has them wrong here, but persists in his tall tales against 1789,” Burck said. “These are personal attacks untethered to actual evidence.”

‘Serendipitous timing’ of investments, Raskin says in letters

The firm was founded in 2022 and Trump Jr. was announced as a partner in November 2024.

In his letters to the four companies obtained by The Associated Press, Raskin outlined how federal policies or contracts had benefited their businesses and claimed that 1789 Capital had suspiciously “serendipitous timing” when it invested in them.

Hadrian Automation, he wrote, received nearly $1 billion in U.S. Navy and Army contracts in March — its first-ever federal contracts — after bringing 1789 Capital on as an investor in 2025.

Juul, Raskin wrote, received Food and Drug Administration clearance to keep its electronic cigarette products on the market in July 2025, four months after 1789 Capital had taken a stake in the company.

The congressman wrote that GrabAGun got help from 1789 to go public and put Trump Jr. on its board before the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives issued a proposed rule to ease the process of shipping guns to people’s homes.

Raskin calls Trump administration order ‘blatantly unlawful’

Raskin also raised questions about the Justice Department and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission closing investigations into Polymarket in July 2025, after 1789 Capital already had invested in the prediction market platform.
GrabAGun said in a statement that Raskin’s letter “is a political document, and its allegations are baseless.”

“ATF’s review of its regulations was well known across the firearms industry, and the agency published numerous proposed rules for public comment. GrabAGun’s only input came through public comments on several of those proposals,” the statement read.

Juul Labs said that it was reviewing its letter closely.

“As always, we intend to cooperate with any Congressional effort to understand our company, our commitment to combating underage vaping, and our mission to help adult smokers of combustible cigarettes transition completely away from smoking,” it said in an emailed response.

The other recipients of the letters didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

The Trump administration has taken steps to push back on the Democrats’ oversight efforts, including an executive order on Friday directing federal contractors and subcontractors to consult with his administration about inquiries they receive from Congress and to withhold any communications that the White House considers privileged.

That could complicate compliance with Raskin’s investigation for at least one of the companies, Hadrian Automation, which is a federal contractor.

Raskin has called Trump’s order “blatantly unlawful” and said that public contractors have a “duty and a right to speak truthfully when Congress calls.”

—Ali Swenson, Associated Press
